entries.title: Use of unassigned local variable
entries.explain: C# insists that every local variable has a value before it is read. The compiler follows every path through your code, and on at least one of them this variable is read before anything was stored in it.
causes: The variable is declared without a value (`int total;`) and only assigned inside an `if`, a loop or a `try`, so one path skips the assignment.
A `switch` or `if`/`else if` chain has no final `else` or `default`, so one case leaves it unassigned.
An `out` argument is read before the method that fills it is called.
fix: Give it a starting value where you declare it: `int total = 0;`.
Or make sure every branch assigns it, for example by adding the missing `else` or `default`.
entries.specific: `{name}` is read before it is assigned{onLine}.

entries.title: The name does not exist in the current context
entries.explain: The compiler cannot find anything called this name from where you use it. Either it is spelled differently where it is declared, or it is declared somewhere this line cannot see, such as inside another block or method.
causes: A typo or a different capital letter: C# names are case-sensitive (`count` and `Count` are different).
The variable was declared inside a block (`if`, loop, `try`) and is used after that block ends.
A missing `using` directive for a type or static class you meant to use.
fix: Check the spelling and casing against the declaration.
Declare the variable before the block, in the scope where you use it.
entries.specific: Nothing called `{name}` is visible{onLine}.

entries.title: Cannot implicitly convert type
entries.explain: C# only converts between types automatically when it is always safe and lossless (an `int` into a `long`). Here the value's type and the target's type are unrelated, such as text and a number, so you must convert it yourself.
causes: Assigning text to a number: `int age = "42";` or `int age = Console.ReadLine();`.
Using `=` instead of `==` in a condition: `if (count = 0)` assigns an `int` where a `bool` is needed.
Returning a value of a different type than the method declares.
fix: Parse text into numbers: `int.Parse(text)` or `int.TryParse(text, out var n)`.
Use `==` to compare inside conditions.
Make the variable's or method's declared type match the value.
entries.before:
string input = "42";
int age = input;   // CS0029
entries.after:
string input = "42";
int age = int.Parse(input);
entries.specific: A `{from}` is used where a `{to}` is needed{onLine}.

entries.title: Cannot implicitly convert type (an explicit conversion exists)
entries.explain: A conversion between these types exists, but it can lose information (a `double` into an `int` drops the fraction; a `long` may not fit in an `int`). C# wants you to say you accept that by writing a cast or choosing a rounding method.
causes: Storing a `double` or `decimal` result in an `int`: `int avg = sum / 2.0;`.
Storing a `long` in an `int`, or an `int` in a `byte`.
Storing a nullable `int?` in a plain `int`.
fix: If dropping the fraction is fine, cast: `(int)value` (it truncates toward zero).
To round instead: `(int)Math.Round(value)`.
Or change the variable's type to the wider one (`double avg`). For `int?`, use `?? 0`.
entries.before:
double price = 9.99;
int cents = price * 100;   // CS0266
entries.after:
double price = 9.99;
int cents = (int)Math.Round(price * 100);
entries.specific: A `{from}` is assigned to a `{to}`{onLine}, which needs an explicit cast.

entries.title: ; expected
entries.explain: Every C# statement ends with a semicolon. The compiler reached the end of a statement (often a line break followed by something new) and found no `;`.
causes: A forgotten `;` at the end of the line, or of the line just before.
An unfinished expression, such as a missing operator between two values.
A keyword typo that makes the compiler read the line differently than you meant.
fix: Add `;` at the end of the reported line; if that line looks right, check the line above.
Fix only the first syntax error and rebuild: one missing character can cause several follow-on errors.
entries.before:
var total = 0
total += 5;   // CS1002 on the line above
entries.after:
var total = 0;
total += 5;
entries.specific: A `;` is missing at the end of the statement{onLine} (or just before it).

entries.title: Syntax error, token expected
entries.explain: The compiler expected a specific punctuation mark at this point, usually a comma between arguments or items, and found something else.
causes: A missing comma between method arguments or collection items: `Math.Max(a b)`.
A missing comma between parameters in a declaration.
A misplaced bracket that makes the compiler lose track of the list.
fix: Add the token named in the message where the compiler points.
Check that brackets and parentheses before this point are balanced.
entries.before: var largest = Math.Max(a b);   // CS1003
entries.after: var largest = Math.Max(a, b);
entries.specific: A `{token}` is expected{onLine}.

entries.title: } expected
entries.explain: A block opened with `{` was never closed. The compiler reached the end of the file (or of an enclosing block) still waiting for the matching `}`.
causes: A forgotten `}` at the end of a method, `if`, loop or class.
An extra `{` somewhere that now needs a partner.
An unclosed string or comment that swallowed the closing brace.
fix: Match each `{` with a `}`: an editor's brace highlighting or auto-format shows where the nesting goes wrong.
The reported line is where the compiler noticed, often the last line; the missing brace is usually earlier.
entries.specific: A `{` opened earlier is still unclosed when the compiler reaches line {line}.

entries.title: Invalid expression term
entries.explain: The compiler expected a value (a number, variable, call or other expression) and found a keyword or symbol that cannot start one, so the expression is incomplete.
causes: Something missing on one side of an operator: `if (x == )` or `total = * 2;`.
An extra or doubled comma or parenthesis.
A statement keyword used where a value belongs, such as `int` on its own.
fix: Look just before the reported token: usually a value is missing there.
Complete the expression or remove the stray symbol.
entries.before:
if (count == )
    Console.WriteLine("none");   // CS1525
entries.after:
if (count == 0)
    Console.WriteLine("none");
entries.specific: `{token}` appears where a value was expected{onLine}.

entries.title: ) expected
entries.explain: A `(` was opened, for a method call, condition or cast, and the compiler reached the end of it without finding the matching `)`.
causes: A missing `)` at the end of a call: `Console.WriteLine("hi";`.
Nested calls where one closing parenthesis was dropped: `Math.Max(a, Math.Min(b, c);`.
A condition such as `if ((a > b)` with one bracket too few.
fix: Count the `(` and `)` on the line; add the missing `)` where the inner call or condition ends.
entries.before: Console.WriteLine(Math.Max(a, b);   // CS1026
entries.after: Console.WriteLine(Math.Max(a, b));
entries.specific: A `)` is missing{onLine}.

entries.title: Identifier expected
entries.explain: The compiler expected a name (of a variable, parameter, method or member) at this point and found something else, such as a symbol, a keyword or nothing.
causes: A parameter with a type but no name: `int Square(int) => ...`.
A name that starts with a digit or uses a reserved keyword, such as `class` or `int` (use `@class` if you must).
A stray `.` with nothing after it.
fix: Give the parameter or variable a name.
Start names with a letter or underscore, and avoid keywords.
entries.before: static int Square(int) => value * value;   // CS1001
entries.after: static int Square(int value) => value * value;
entries.specific: A name is missing{onLine}.

entries.capture: '(?<member>[^']+)': not all code paths return a value
entries.title: Not all code paths return a value
entries.explain: A method that declares a return type must end in a `return` (or `throw`) on every possible path. The compiler found a path, often the one where no `if` matched or a loop never ran, that falls off the end with nothing to return.
causes: An `if` with a `return` but no `else` and no `return` after it.
A `return` only inside a loop, which might run zero times.
A `switch` whose cases all return, but without a `default`.
fix: Add a final `return` after the `if` or loop for the remaining case.
Or add the missing `else` / `default`, or `throw` if that case is truly impossible.
entries.specific: `{member}` can reach its end without returning a value.

entries.capture: Operator '(?<op>[^']+)' cannot be applied to operands of type '(?<left>[^']+)' and '(?<right>[^']+)'
entries.title: Operator cannot be applied to operands of these types
entries.explain: The operator has no meaning for this combination of types. For example `-` is defined for numbers but not for a `string` and an `int`, and `&&` needs two `bool` values.
causes: Doing math with text: `"5" - 2` (only `+` works with strings, and it joins them).
Comparing values of unrelated types, such as a `string` with an `int`.
Using `&&` or `||` with numbers, or forgetting `()` on a method call so you are using a method group.
fix: Convert first: `int.Parse(text) - 2`.
Compare like with like, such as `number == int.Parse(text)` or `number.ToString() == text`.
Call methods with `()`.
entries.before:
string input = "10";
int left = input - 3;   // CS0019
entries.after:
string input = "10";
int left = int.Parse(input) - 3;
entries.specific: `{op}` cannot be used between a `{left}` and a `{right}`{onLine}.

entries.capture: '(?<type>[^']+)' does not contain a definition for '(?<name>[^']+)'
entries.title: Type does not contain a definition
entries.explain: You used a member through a type name (a static member, like `Console.WriteLine` or `Math.Max`) and that type has no member with this exact name.
causes: A spelling or casing slip: `Console.Writeline`, `Math.max`.
Expecting a member that belongs to a different type (`Math.Parse` instead of `int.Parse`).
Your own class and the member is not declared, or not `static`.
fix: Fix the spelling and casing; let the editor's completion list show what exists.
Check the member really lives on that type.
entries.before: Console.Writeline("Hello");   // CS0117
entries.after: Console.WriteLine("Hello");
entries.specific: `{type}` has nothing called `{name}`{onLine}.

entries.capture: '(?<type>[^']+)' does not contain a definition for '(?<name>[^']+)'
entries.title: Type does not contain a definition (or extension method)
entries.explain: The value's type has no property or method with this name, and no extension method with that name is in scope. Members are looked up on the declared type of the variable, not on what you hope it contains.
causes: Using a member from another type: `list.Length` (lists have `Count`), `array.Count` (arrays have `Length`), `text.Size`.
A typo or casing slip: `name.length`, `list.add`.
The variable's declared type is a base type or interface that lacks the member.
An extension method whose namespace is not imported with `using`.
fix: Use the member that type really has (`Count` for `List<T>`, `Length` for arrays and strings).
Fix the casing: .NET members are PascalCase (`Add`, `Length`).
Add the `using` for the extension method's namespace.
entries.before:
var names = new List<string> { "Ann", "Bo" };
Console.WriteLine(names.Length);   // CS1061
entries.after:
var names = new List<string> { "Ann", "Bo" };
Console.WriteLine(names.Count);
entries.specific: A `{type}` has no member called `{name}`{onLine}.

entries.capture: type or namespace name '(?<name>[^']+)' could not be found
entries.title: The type or namespace name could not be found
entries.explain: The compiler does not know a type with this name. Either it is misspelled, it is defined in a namespace you have not imported with `using`, or it lives in a package or project that is not referenced.
causes: A typo or casing slip: `Stringbuilder`, `list<int>`.
A missing `using`: `StringBuilder` needs `using System.Text;`, `Regex` needs `using System.Text.RegularExpressions;`.
A class you meant to write but have not declared yet, or a NuGet package that is not installed.
fix: Check spelling and casing against the docs.
Add the right `using` at the top of the file.
Declare the class, or add the package reference.
entries.before:
var sb = new StringBuilder();   // CS0246: no using System.Text
sb.Append("hi");
entries.specific: No type called `{name}` is visible{onLine}.

entries.capture: type or namespace name '(?<name>[^']+)' does not exist in the namespace '(?<ns>[^']+)'
entries.title: The type or namespace does not exist in the namespace
entries.explain: A qualified name such as `System.Collection.Generic` names a part that does not exist inside the namespace before it. Usually one segment is misspelled.
causes: A typo in a `using` directive: `System.Collection.Generic` (it is `Collections`).
A type assumed to live in a namespace where it does not.
A missing package that would add types to that namespace.
fix: Check each segment of the name against the docs.
Let the editor suggest the right `using` from the type name.
entries.before: using System.Collection.Generic;   // CS0234
entries.after: using System.Collections.Generic;
entries.specific: `{ns}` has no `{name}` inside it{onLine}.

entries.title: A local variable is already defined in this scope
entries.explain: Each name can be declared only once in a scope. Writing `var x = ...` (or `int x = ...`) a second time declares a new variable, and the compiler refuses a second one with the same name.
causes: Repeating the type or `var` when you only meant to change the value.
Copying a block of code that declares the same variable.
Two pattern variables (`is int n`) with the same name in one scope.
fix: To change the existing variable, assign without the type: `total = 5;`.
If you really need two variables, give them different names.
entries.before:
var total = 0;
var total = total + 5;   // CS0128
entries.after:
var total = 0;
total = total + 5;
entries.specific: `{name}` is declared a second time{onLine}.

entries.capture: named '(?<name>[^']+)' cannot be declared in this scope
entries.title: A local cannot be declared here: the name is used in an enclosing scope
entries.explain: C# does not let an inner block declare a variable with the same name as one in an enclosing block, because it would be unclear which one the name means.
causes: A loop variable that repeats an outer variable: `var i = 0; for (var i = 0; ...)`.
A lambda parameter or `out var` with the same name as a local outside it.
Declaring the variable inside a block and again after it in the outer scope.
fix: Rename the inner variable.
Or reuse the outer one without declaring it again.
entries.specific: `{name}` is already used by an enclosing scope{onLine}.

entries.capture: local variable '(?<name>[^']+)' before it is declared
entries.title: Cannot use local variable before it is declared
entries.explain: Local variables exist from their declaration onward. The name is declared later in the same block, so on this line it cannot be used yet.
causes: Lines in the wrong order: using the variable, then declaring it below.
Code moved or pasted above the declaration.
In top-level statements, a variable declared below the code that reads it.
fix: Move the declaration above the first line that uses it.
entries.before:
Console.WriteLine(greeting);   // CS0841
var greeting = "Hi";
entries.after:
var greeting = "Hi";
Console.WriteLine(greeting);
entries.specific: `{name}` is used{onLine} before the line that declares it.

entries.title: An object reference is required for the non-static member
entries.explain: An instance (non-static) member belongs to each object of the class, so it needs an object to work on. The code used it from a `static` method, or through the class name, where there is no object.
causes: Calling an instance method or field from `static void Main` in the same class.
Writing `ClassName.Member` for a member that is not `static`.
Declaring a helper method without `static` while calling it from static code.
fix: If the member does not need per-object data, mark it `static`.
Otherwise create an object and use it: `var c = new Counter(); c.Increment();`.
entries.specific: `{member}` needs an object to be used through{onLine}.

entries.capture: Cannot assign (?<what>.+?) to an implicitly-typed variable
entries.title: Cannot assign this to an implicitly-typed variable
entries.explain: `var` takes its type from the value on the right. Some values have no type of their own, such as `null` or a lambda with nothing to infer from, so `var` cannot pick one.
causes: `var name = null;`
`var f = x => x * 2;` where the parameter type cannot be worked out.
Assigning a `void` method call, which produces no value.
fix: Write the type: `string? name = null;`.
Give lambda parameters a type: `var f = (int x) => x * 2;`, or use `Func<int, int>`.
entries.before: var winner = null;   // CS0815
entries.after: string? winner = null;
entries.specific: `var` cannot work out a type from `{what}`{onLine}.

entries.title: Implicitly-typed variables must be initialized
entries.explain: `var` has no type of its own: it copies the type of the value you assign in the declaration. Without a value there is nothing to copy.
causes: Declaring with `var x;` and assigning later.
Declaring before an `if` that sets the value in each branch.
fix: Assign in the declaration: `var total = 0;`.
Or write the type explicitly: `int total;`.
entries.before:
var label;   // CS0818
label = "ok";
entries.after:
string label;
label = "ok";
entries.specific: A `var` declaration{onLine} has no value to take its type from.

entries.capture: No overload for method '(?<name>[^']+)' takes (?<count>\d+) arguments
entries.title: No overload for method takes this many arguments
entries.explain: The method exists, but none of its versions (overloads) accepts the number of arguments you passed.
causes: Passing too many or too few arguments: `Math.Max(a, b, c)` (it takes two).
Calling your own method after changing its parameter list.
A misplaced parenthesis that moves an argument into the wrong call.
fix: Check the method's parameters (hover it in the editor) and pass that many.
To combine more values, nest calls or use LINQ: `new[] { a, b, c }.Max()`.
entries.before: var largest = Math.Max(4, 9, 2);   // CS1501
entries.after: var largest = new[] { 4, 9, 2 }.Max();
entries.specific: `{name}` has no version that takes {count} arguments{onLine}.

entries.title: Argument cannot convert from one type to another
entries.explain: One argument has a type the method's parameter does not accept, and there is no automatic conversion between them. The argument number says which one, counting from 1.
causes: Passing text where a number is expected (or the other way round).
Arguments in the wrong order.
Passing a method name without `()`, or a `List<T>` where an array is required.
fix: Convert the value: `int.Parse(text)`, `number.ToString()`, `list.ToArray()`.
Check the order of the parameters.
entries.before:
static int Square(int n) => n * n;
Console.WriteLine(Square("4"));   // CS1503
entries.after:
static int Square(int n) => n * n;
Console.WriteLine(Square(4));
entries.specific: Argument {pos} is a `{from}`, but the parameter needs a `{to}`{onLine}.

entries.title: There is no argument given for a required parameter
entries.explain: The method or constructor has a parameter without a default value, and the call does not pass anything for it.
causes: Calling a method with fewer arguments than it declares.
`new Person()` when the class only has a constructor that takes values (declaring any constructor removes the default empty one).
Deriving from a class whose constructor needs arguments without calling `: base(...)`.
fix: Pass a value for the parameter.
Or give the parameter a default (`string name = "guest"`), or add a parameterless constructor.
entries.before:
static void Greet(string name) => Console.WriteLine($"Hi {name}");
Greet();   // CS7036
entries.after:
static void Greet(string name) => Console.WriteLine($"Hi {name}");
Greet("Ann");
entries.specific: Nothing is passed for `{param}` of `{member}`{onLine}.

entries.capture: '(?<type>[^']+)' does not contain a constructor that takes (?<count>\d+) arguments
entries.title: Type does not contain a constructor that takes this many arguments
entries.explain: `new` passed a number of arguments that no constructor of the class accepts.
causes: Passing values for properties the class has, but no constructor that takes them.
Calling `new` with extra or missing arguments after the constructor changed.
Confusing constructor arguments with an object initializer `{ Name = ... }`.
fix: Pass the arguments the existing constructor expects.
Or set settable properties with an initializer: `new Person { Name = "Ann", Age = 30 }`.
Or add a constructor (or use a `record Person(string Name, int Age)`).
entries.before:
var p = new Person("Ann", 30);   // CS1729

class Person { public string Name = ""; public int Age; }
entries.after:
var p = new Person { Name = "Ann", Age = 30 };

class Person { public string Name = ""; public int Age; }
entries.specific: `{type}` has no constructor that takes {count} arguments{onLine}.

entries.capture: Property or indexer '(?<name>[^']+)' cannot be assigned to
entries.title: Property cannot be assigned to: it is read only
entries.explain: The property has a getter but no setter (or the indexer has no `set`), so values can be read but not stored. Get-only auto-properties can be set only in a constructor or initializer.
causes: Assigning a get-only property, such as `{ get; }` or `=> ...`, from outside the constructor.
Trying to change a built-in read-only property, such as `text.Length` or `list.Count`.
Setting a character in a string with `text[0] = 'x'` (strings cannot be changed).
fix: Add a setter: `{ get; set; }`, or `{ get; init; }` to allow it only in object initializers.
Set it in the constructor.
For strings, build a new one (`"X" + text[1..]`).
entries.after:
var b = new Box { Size = 3 };

class Box { public int Size { get; init; } }
entries.specific: `{name}` is read-only{onLine}.

entries.title: A readonly field cannot be assigned to
entries.explain: A `readonly` field can be set only where it is declared or in a constructor of its own class. Assigning it anywhere else, such as in a normal method, is refused so the value stays fixed after construction.
causes: Changing a `readonly` field in a method.
Setting it from outside the class.
Marking a field `readonly` that really does need to change.
fix: Assign it in the constructor.
If it must change later, remove `readonly`.
entries.specific: A `readonly` field is assigned outside a constructor{onLine}.

entries.title: The left-hand side of an assignment must be a variable, property or indexer
entries.explain: `=` stores a value into the thing on its left, so the left side must be somewhere a value can be stored. A calculation, a method's return value or a literal is just a value, not a storage place.
causes: Writing the assignment backwards, as in maths: `total * 2 = result;`.
Assigning to a method call: `GetName() = "Bo";`.
Using `=` where `==` was meant in an expression.
fix: Put the variable on the left: `result = total * 2;`.
Compare with `==`.
entries.before:
int result = 0;
price * 2 = result;   // CS0131
entries.after:
int result = 0;
result = price * 2;
entries.specific: The left side of `=`{onLine} is not something a value can be stored in.

entries.title: Only assignment, call, increment, decrement, await, and new can be used as a statement
entries.explain: A statement must do something: assign, call a method, increment, await or create an object. A bare value or comparison on its own line computes something and throws it away, which C# treats as a mistake.
causes: `count + 1;` instead of `count += 1;` or `count++;`.
`x == 5;` where `x = 5;` was meant.
A property or method name without `()`: `list.Clear;`.
fix: Store the result (`count = count + 1;`), or use the assignment operator you meant.
Add `()` to call a method.
entries.before:
int count = 0;
count + 1;   // CS0201
entries.after:
int count = 0;
count += 1;
entries.specific: The statement{onLine} computes a value but does nothing with it.

entries.title: A void method cannot return a value
entries.explain: The method is declared `void`, meaning it returns nothing, yet it has `return something;`. Either the method should return that type, or the `return` should be bare.
causes: Forgetting to change `void` to the real return type.
Writing `return x;` in a method that only should print or change state.
fix: Change `void` to the type you return (`int`, `string`, ...).
Or write `return;` with no value.
entries.specific: `{member}` is `void`, but returns a value{onLine}.

entries.title: An object of the return type is required
entries.explain: The method promises to return a value, but this `return;` has no value. Every `return` in a non-void method must give back something of the declared type.
causes: A bare `return;` used to exit early from a method that returns a value.
Changing a method from `void` to a type without updating its `return` statements.
fix: Return a value of the right type: `return 0;`, `return null;` (for nullable types), `return "";`.
Or make the method `void` if it should not return anything.
entries.specific: A `return`{onLine} needs a `{type}` value.

entries.title: Cannot convert type
entries.explain: A cast like `(int)value` only works between types that are related, such as two number types or a class and its subclass. A `string` and an `int` are unrelated, so no cast exists: you have to parse or format instead.
causes: Casting text to a number: `(int)"42"`.
Casting a number to text: `(string)42`.
Casting between two unrelated classes.
fix: Parse text: `int.Parse("42")`.
Format numbers: `42.ToString()`.
entries.before:
string input = "42";
int n = (int)input;   // CS0030
entries.after:
string input = "42";
int n = int.Parse(input);
entries.specific: There is no cast from `{from}` to `{to}`{onLine}.

entries.title: Cannot apply indexing with [] to this type
entries.explain: Square brackets read an item by position or key, which works for arrays, strings, lists and dictionaries. This value's type has no indexer, so `[ ]` means nothing for it.
causes: Indexing a number to get a digit: `n[0]` on an `int`.
Indexing an `IEnumerable<T>` (a LINQ result), which has no indexer.
Indexing a method group by forgetting `()`.
fix: For digits, go through text: `n.ToString()[0]`, or use `% 10` and `/ 10`.
For LINQ results, use `.ElementAt(i)` or call `.ToList()` first.
entries.before:
int year = 2025;
char first = year[0];   // CS0021
entries.after:
int year = 2025;
char first = year.ToString()[0];
entries.specific: A `{type}` cannot be indexed with `[]`{onLine}.

entries.title: Cannot convert method group: did you intend to invoke the method?
entries.explain: A method name without parentheses refers to the method itself (a "method group"), not its result. You forgot the `()` that calls it.
causes: `string s = x.ToString;` instead of `x.ToString()`.
Reading a method's result without calling it: `text.Trim`, `number.ToString`, `DateTime.Now.ToShortDateString`.
fix: Add `()` to call the method.
entries.before:
var name = " Ann ";
string clean = name.Trim;   // CS0428
entries.after:
var name = " Ann ";
string clean = name.Trim();
entries.specific: `{name}` is used without `()`{onLine}, so it is the method itself, not a `{to}`.

entries.title: Non-invocable member cannot be used like a method
entries.explain: The name is a property or field, not a method, so it cannot be called with `()`. Read it without parentheses.
causes: `text.Length()` (it is the property `text.Length`).
`list.Count()` works through LINQ, but `array.Length()` and `dict.Keys()` do not.
Calling your own property as if it were a method.
fix: Remove the `()`: `text.Length`.
entries.before:
var word = "hello";
Console.WriteLine(word.Length());   // CS1955
entries.after:
var word = "hello";
Console.WriteLine(word.Length);
entries.specific: `{member}` is a property or field, so it is read without `()`{onLine}.

entries.capture: '(?<name>[^']+)' is a (?<kind>\w+), which is not valid in the given context
entries.title: Name is a type or method, which is not valid in this context
entries.explain: The name refers to something that cannot be used as a value here. A class name is a type, not an object, and a method name needs `()` to produce a value.
causes: Using a class name where an object is needed: `var p = Person;` instead of `new Person()`.
Using a type name as a value, such as `Console.WriteLine(int);`.
A variable with the same name as a type, where the type wins.
fix: Create an object with `new Type()`, or use a variable that holds one.
Call methods with `()`.
entries.before:
var p = Person;   // CS0119

class Person { }
entries.after:
var p = new Person();

class Person { }
entries.specific: `{name}` is a {kind}, not a value{onLine}.

entries.title: A constant value is expected
entries.explain: Some places only accept values known when the code compiles, such as a `case` label in a `switch`. A variable's value is only known at run time, so it cannot be used there.
causes: Using a variable as a `case` label: `case limit:`.
An array size together with an initializer list where the size is a variable.
fix: Use a `const` (`const int Limit = 10;`) or a literal.
For run-time values, use a `when` guard or an `if`: `case int n when n == limit:`.
entries.specific: A value that is not a constant is used where one is required{onLine}.

entries.title: Control cannot fall through from one case label to another
entries.explain: In C#, each `switch` section must end with `break`, `return`, `throw` or `goto`. Unlike C or JavaScript, running on into the next `case` silently is not allowed.
causes: A `case` section without `break;` at the end.
Expecting two cases to share code by falling through from one to the next.
fix: End the section with `break;` (or `return`).
To share code, stack labels with no code between them: `case 1: case 2: ...`, or use a switch expression or `or` pattern (`case 1 or 2:`).
entries.specific: The `{label}` section runs into the next case without a `break`.

entries.title: Type of conditional expression cannot be determined
entries.explain: Both results of `condition ? a : b` must share a type the compiler can settle on. Here the two branches have unrelated types, and nothing around the expression (such as `var`) tells it which type you want.
causes: Mixing a number and text: `ok ? 1 : "none"`.
Mixing `null` with a value type when using `var`: `var x = ok ? 5 : null;`.
Two different classes with no common type stated.
fix: Make both branches the same type: `ok ? "1" : "none"`.
Or declare the target type instead of `var`: `int? x = ok ? 5 : null;`.
entries.before: var label = count > 0 ? count : "none";   // CS0173
entries.after: var label = count > 0 ? count.ToString() : "none";
entries.specific: The two branches of `?:`{onLine} are a `{a}` and a `{b}`.

entries.title: The type caught or thrown must be derived from System.Exception
entries.explain: Only exception objects can be thrown or caught in C#: their class must inherit from `System.Exception`, which carries the message and stack trace.
causes: Throwing an object of your own class that does not inherit from `Exception`.
Writing `catch (string message)` or `catch (int code)`.
fix: Make your class inherit from `Exception`: `class NotFoundException(string msg) : Exception(msg);`.
Or throw a built-in one: `throw new InvalidOperationException("...");`.
entries.before:
throw new NotFound();   // CS0155

class NotFound { }
entries.after:
throw new NotFoundException("No such item");

class NotFoundException(string message) : Exception(message);
entries.specific: Something that is not an `Exception` is thrown or caught{onLine}.

entries.title: Not all code paths return a value in lambda expression
entries.explain: A lambda with a block body `{ ... }` that should produce a value must `return` on every path. One path, often the end of an `if`, runs off the end without returning.
causes: An `if` with a `return` but no `else` or final `return`.
A `return` only inside a loop.
fix: Add a final `return` for the remaining case.
Or write the lambda as a single expression: `x => x > 0 ? "pos" : "neg"`.
entries.specific: A path through the `{type}` lambda{onLine} ends without a `return`.

entries.title: The out parameter must be assigned before control leaves the method
entries.explain: An `out` parameter is a promise to the caller that the method will fill it in. Every path out of the method, including early `return`s, must assign it.
causes: An early `return false;` before the `out` value is set.
Assigning it only inside an `if`.
fix: Assign a default at the top of the method: `result = 0;`.
Or assign it on each path before `return`.
entries.specific: `{name}` is not assigned on every path out of the method.

entries.title: 'await' can only be used within an async method
entries.explain: `await` pauses a method until a task finishes, which only works in a method (or lambda) marked `async`. An async method must also return `Task`, `Task<T>` (or `ValueTask`) instead of a plain value or `void`.
causes: Calling `await` inside a method that is not marked `async`.
Using `await` inside a lambda that is not `async`, for example in `Select` or an event handler.
Adding `await` to existing code without updating the method signature.
fix: Mark the method `async` and change its return type: `int` becomes `Task<int>`, `void` becomes `Task`.
Then `await` the method where it is called. Top-level statements may use `await` directly.
For lambdas, write `async () => ...`.
entries.specific: `await` is used{onLine} in a method or lambda that is not `async`.

entries.title: Class does not implement interface member
entries.explain: A class that lists an interface promises to provide every member the interface declares (unless the interface gives a default body). One of them is missing, or its signature does not match exactly.
causes: A member not written yet.
A different name, parameter list or return type than the interface declares.
The member is not `public` (implicit implementations must be public).
fix: Add the member with exactly the interface's signature, as `public`.
Editors offer "Implement interface" to generate the missing members.
entries.before:
interface IShape { double Area(); }
class Square : IShape { }   // CS0535
entries.specific: `{type}` is missing `{member}`.

entries.capture: '(?<type>[^']+)' does not implement inherited abstract member '(?<member>[^']+)'
entries.title: Class does not implement inherited abstract member
entries.explain: The base class declares an `abstract` member, which has no body and must be supplied by every non-abstract class that derives from it. This class does not supply it with `override`.
causes: The member was not written in the derived class.
It was written without `override`, or with a different signature.
fix: Add the member with `public override` and the same signature.
Or mark the derived class `abstract` too, if it is not meant to be created directly.
entries.before:
abstract class Shape { public abstract double Area(); }
class Circle : Shape { }   // CS0534
entries.specific: `{type}` must override `{member}`.

entries.title: Cannot override: the inherited member is not virtual, abstract, or override
entries.explain: In C#, methods cannot be overridden unless the base class allows it by marking them `virtual` or `abstract`. The base member here is a plain method, so `override` has nothing to replace.
causes: Forgetting `virtual` on the base class method.
Trying to override a method of a class you do not own that is not virtual.
fix: Mark the base method `virtual` (or `abstract`).
If you cannot change the base class, use a different design, such as wrapping it.
entries.before:
class Animal { public string Speak() => "..."; }
class Dog : Animal { public override string Speak() => "Woof"; }   // CS0506
entries.after:
class Animal { public virtual string Speak() => "..."; }
class Dog : Animal { public override string Speak() => "Woof"; }
entries.specific: `{member}` is not `virtual`, so it cannot be overridden{onLine}.

entries.title: Cannot create an instance of an abstract type or interface
entries.explain: An interface or `abstract` class describes what something must do, but is not complete on its own, so `new` cannot create one. Create an object of a concrete class that implements or derives from it.
causes: `new IShape()` or `new Shape()` where `Shape` is `abstract`.
`new IList<int>()` instead of `new List<int>()`.
fix: Create a concrete class: `IShape s = new Square(2);`, `IList<int> xs = new List<int>();`.
entries.before: IList<int> numbers = new IList<int>();   // CS0144
entries.after: IList<int> numbers = new List<int>();
entries.specific: `{type}` cannot be created with `new`{onLine}.

entries.title: A field initializer cannot reference a non-static member
entries.explain: Field initializers run before the constructor, while the object is still being set up, so they may not read other instance fields, properties or methods. C# forbids it to avoid depending on initialization order.
causes: `int b = a + 1;` where `a` is another instance field.
Calling an instance method in a field initializer.
fix: Compute the value in the constructor.
Or make the referenced member `static` or `const`, or turn the field into a computed property: `int B => A + 1;`.
entries.specific: A field initializer{onLine} reads `{member}`, which does not exist yet at that point.

entries.title: Top-level statements must precede namespace and type declarations
entries.explain: With top-level statements (a program without `static void Main`), the statements must come first in the file. Classes, records and other types go after them.
causes: A class declared at the top of `Program.cs`, with statements below it.
Statements added at the bottom of the file after the type declarations.
fix: Move all statements above the first `class`, `record`, `struct`, `enum` or `namespace`.
entries.specific: A statement{onLine} comes after a type declaration; move it above.

entries.capture: '(?<member>[^']+)' is inaccessible due to its protection level
entries.title: Member is inaccessible due to its protection level
entries.explain: The member exists, but it is `private` (the default for class members) or `protected` / `internal`, so code outside its class cannot use it.
causes: A field or method declared without an access modifier, which makes it `private`.
Reaching into another class's private data instead of using its public members.
fix: Use a public member the class offers (such as a property).
Or, if it should be part of the class's public face, mark it `public`.
entries.specific: `{member}` is not accessible from here{onLine}.

entries.title: Type already defines a member with the same parameter types
entries.explain: Two methods with the same name must differ in their parameter types (overloading). These two have identical parameter types; a different return type or different parameter names are not enough to tell them apart.
causes: The same method pasted twice.
Two overloads that differ only in return type or parameter names.
fix: Delete the duplicate.
Or rename one of them, or change its parameter types.
entries.specific: `{type}` already has a `{name}` with these parameter types{onLine}.

entries.title: Newline in constant
entries.explain: A normal string literal (`"..."`) or character literal must be closed on the same line it starts. The line ended before the closing quote.
causes: A missing closing `"`.
A string meant to span lines; regular strings cannot contain a raw line break.
A `\` before the closing quote (`"C:\temp\"`), which escapes the quote instead of ending the string.
fix: Close the quote on the same line.
For multi-line text, use a raw string literal `"""..."""` or write `\n`.
For paths, use a verbatim string: `@"C:\temp\"`.
entries.before:
var greeting = "Hello;
Console.WriteLine(greeting);
entries.after:
var greeting = "Hello";
Console.WriteLine(greeting);
entries.specific: A string or character literal{onLine} is not closed before the line ends.

entries.title: Too many characters in character literal
entries.explain: Single quotes make a `char`, which holds exactly one character. Text with more than one character is a `string` and needs double quotes.
causes: Writing strings in single quotes, as in Python or JavaScript: `'hello'`.
Two characters in a `char`, such as `'ab'`.
fix: Use double quotes for text: `"hello"`.
Keep single quotes for one character: `'h'`.
entries.before: string name = 'Ann';   // CS1012
entries.after: string name = "Ann";
entries.specific: Single quotes{onLine} contain more than one character; use double quotes for a string.

entries.title: Converting null literal or possible null value to non-nullable type
entries.explain: Nullable reference types are on, so `string` means "never null" and `string?` means "may be null". A value that may be `null` (or the literal `null`) is stored into a variable declared as never null. This is a warning, but it points at a likely `NullReferenceException`.
causes: `string name = Console.ReadLine();` (it returns `string?`, `null` at end of input).
Storing the result of `FirstOrDefault()`, `Find()` or `as` in a non-nullable variable.
`string s = null;`
fix: Declare the variable as nullable (`string? name`) and check it before use.
Or provide a fallback: `Console.ReadLine() ?? ""`.
entries.before: string name = Console.ReadLine();   // CS8600
entries.after: string name = Console.ReadLine() ?? "";
entries.specific: A possibly null value is stored in a non-nullable variable{onLine}.

entries.title: Dereference of a possibly null reference
entries.explain: The compiler's null analysis sees that this variable may be `null` here, and you are using a member on it (`.Length`, `.Name`, a method call). If it really is `null` at run time, that line throws `NullReferenceException`.
causes: Using the result of `FirstOrDefault()`, `Find()`, `Console.ReadLine()` or a dictionary lookup without checking it.
A `string?` parameter or property used directly.
A check for `null` that the compiler cannot see (it happened in another method).
fix: Check first: `if (item is null) return;` and the compiler will know it is safe after that.
Or use `?.` with a fallback: `item?.Name ?? "none"`.
Only use `!` when you truly know it cannot be `null`.
entries.before:
var line = Console.ReadLine();
Console.WriteLine(line.Length);   // CS8602
entries.specific: A value that may be `null` is used{onLine}.

entries.title: Possible null reference return
entries.explain: The method's return type says it never returns `null` (for example `string` or `Person`), but this `return` may hand back `null`.
causes: `return null;` to signal "not found".
Returning the result of `FirstOrDefault()` or `Find()`.
fix: If "not found" is a real outcome, make the return type nullable: `Person?`, and let callers check.
Otherwise return a real value or throw an exception.
entries.before:
static string FindName(List<string> names) =>
    names.FirstOrDefault(n => n.StartsWith("A"));   // CS8603
entries.after:
static string? FindName(List<string> names) =>
    names.FirstOrDefault(n => n.StartsWith("A"));
entries.specific: The `return`{onLine} may give back `null` from a method that promises not to.

entries.title: Possible null reference argument
entries.explain: A value that may be `null` is passed to a parameter that does not accept `null`. If it is `null` at run time, the method will most likely throw `ArgumentNullException` or `NullReferenceException`.
causes: `int.Parse(Console.ReadLine())`: `ReadLine` may return `null`.
Passing a `string?` variable or a `FirstOrDefault()` result straight into a method.
fix: Check for `null` before the call, or supply a fallback with `??`.
For parsing input, prefer `int.TryParse(Console.ReadLine(), out var n)`, which accepts `null`.
entries.before: int age = int.Parse(Console.ReadLine());   // CS8604
entries.after: int.TryParse(Console.ReadLine(), out int age);
entries.specific: The value passed as `{param}` to `{member}` may be `null`{onLine}.

entries.title: Non-nullable member must contain a non-null value when exiting constructor
entries.explain: The member's type says it is never `null` (such as `string`), but after the constructor finishes nothing has set it, so it would still be `null`.
causes: A `string` or class-typed property with no initializer and no constructor that sets it.
A class that is filled in later by an object initializer or a library, which the compiler cannot see.
fix: Give it a value: `public string Name { get; set; } = "";`.
Or mark it `required` so every `new` must set it: `public required string Name { get; set; }`.
Or make it nullable (`string?`) if it may truly be missing.
entries.specific: The {kind} `{name}` can still be `null` after construction.

entries.title: Cannot convert null literal to non-nullable reference type
entries.explain: The literal `null` is used where the type says it may never be `null`, such as an argument for a `string` parameter or a default value for a `string` field.
causes: Passing `null` to a method whose parameter is `string` rather than `string?`.
A field or parameter default `= null` on a non-nullable type.
fix: If `null` is meaningful, make the type nullable: `string? note = null`.
Otherwise use a real value, such as `""`.
entries.before: static void Log(string message, string tag = null) { }   // CS8625
entries.after: static void Log(string message, string? tag = null) { }
entries.specific: `null` is used{onLine} where the type does not allow it.

entries.title: Possible null reference assignment
entries.explain: A value that may be `null` is assigned to a property, field or array element whose type says it is never `null`.
causes: Assigning a `string?` (such as `Console.ReadLine()`) to a `string` property.
Assigning the result of `FirstOrDefault()` to a non-nullable field.
fix: Add a fallback: `person.Name = input ?? "";`.
Or check for `null` before assigning, or make the target nullable.
entries.before: person.Name = Console.ReadLine();   // CS8601
entries.after: person.Name = Console.ReadLine() ?? "unknown";
entries.specific: A possibly null value is assigned to a non-nullable target{onLine}.

entries.title: Nullable value type may be null
entries.explain: A nullable value type such as `int?` is read with `.Value` (or cast to `int`) where the compiler cannot see that it has a value. If it is `null`, this throws `InvalidOperationException` at run time.
causes: Reading `.Value` without checking `.HasValue`.
Casting `(int)maybe` without a check.
fix: Check first: `if (age is int a) ...` or `if (age.HasValue) ...`.
Or use a fallback: `age ?? 0`.
entries.before:
int? age = FindAge();
int years = age.Value;   // CS8629
entries.after:
int? age = FindAge();
int years = age ?? 0;
entries.specific: A nullable value is read{onLine} without checking that it has one.
